title: How Cremation Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explain how cremation works, from pre-cremation coroner checks and removal of pacemakers and implants, through the flame process in a retort and the cremulator grinding of bone, to what the remains are and how they are handled. They cover cremation history (China since about 8000 BC, the French Revolution Freemasons, Professor Brunetti's crematory and Pennsylvania's 1876 start), crematorium construction and maintenance, the cremated remains (ashes) shipping rules, identification and mix-up risks, and crematory scandals in Georgia (Tri-State Crematory), Pennsylvania, California, and Mississippi. They discuss whether cremation is green compared with burial and biocremation, religious attitudes toward cremation (Hinduism, Islam, Judaism, Catholicism, Protestantism, Mormonism, Eastern Orthodoxy), options for remains (columbarium, scattering, memorial fireworks, coral reefs, diamonds, paintings), scattering rules in national parks and at sea, cremation rates by country, and pet cremation. Listener mail follows at the end.

segments.title: Opening banter and Ralph White
segments.summary: Hosts joke around and discuss Ralph White's posthumous adventures, with friends scattering his remains on travels and in space, and note cremation's portability.

segments.title: History of cremation
segments.summary: Cremation dates to prehistoric times, with China cited from about 8000 BC. The Freemasons during the French Revolution promoted cremation in opposition to the Catholic Church, which had long prohibited it. The modern cremation chamber was invented in the late 1800s by Professor Brunetti, and cremation started in earnest in the US in Pennsylvania in 1876.

segments.title: Cremation rates and reasons for cremating
segments.summary: Hosts note the rising US cremation rate, about 36 percent with an expected rise to half, and cite land scarcity and the environmental concerns of burial as reasons.

segments.title: Pre-cremation steps and removing implants
segments.summary: The body is stored in a cool room and examined by a coroner, who must approve it because exhumation is not possible later. Pacemakers, silicone breast implants, prostheses, and radioactive cancer seeds are removed, while mercury fillings, jewelry, and glasses usually stay in.

segments.title: The cremation process: retort, flame, and bone
segments.summary: The body is placed in a cardboard or pine container and slid into a retort preheated to about 1100 degrees Fahrenheit, with a jet flame aimed at the torso. The body dries, skin blisters, muscles char and can cause limbs to move. Bones calcify and are then swept into a cremulator that grinds them into coarse powder. The process takes about two to three hours, and modern machines are faster. Remains come to about three to nine pounds.

segments.title: Crematorium construction and emissions control
segments.summary: Furnaces are lined with specialized composite brick because of heat up to about 2000 degrees; bricks are replaced after losing about half their width. Units cost around $250,000 and run on gas, propane, or diesel, formerly coal. A second flame burns off dust, and some use water scrubbing.

segments.title: Shipping remains and avoiding mix-ups
segments.summary: The term cremains is disfavored by the industry. Remains can be mailed by USPS in a sift-proof box, but not via FedEx or UPS. Metal ID tags and paperwork are used to prevent mix-ups, though small mixing can happen.

segments.title: Crematory scandals: Georgia, Pennsylvania, California, Mississippi
segments.summary: Brent Marsh's Tri-State Crematory in Noble, Georgia, left bodies half-buried after the incinerator broke, with 336 bodies found; he pleaded guilty and was sentenced to about 12 years after facing theft and abuse of corpse charges. A Pennsylvania operator kept fetal and infant remains in his garage. A California owner sold body parts, and a Mississippi operator, Mark Sieep, mixed remains and dumped ashes. Regulation varies by state, with several states not licensing crematoriums.

segments.title: Is cremation green? Biocremation
segments.summary: Regular cremation uses large amounts of natural gas or electricity and releases about 880 pounds of CO2 per body. Burial has different environmental costs. Biocremation (alkaline hydrolysis) is mentioned as a greener alternative that turns the body into liquid.

segments.title: Religious attitudes toward cremation
segments.summary: Hinduism mandates cremation, with open-air cremations along the Ganges in Varanasi. Sikhism and Jainism strongly favor it. Islam and Orthodox Judaism prohibit it or frown on it, with the Holocaust memory cited for some Jews. Protestants are generally open. The Catholic Church relaxed its stance in the 1960s, and about a third of Catholics are now cremated. Mormons discourage it and Eastern Orthodoxy opposes it.

segments.title: Options for remains: columbarium, fireworks, reefs, diamonds
segments.summary: Options include keeping ashes in an urn, a columbarium, memorial fireworks (Hunter S. Thompson shot from a cannon), space scattering through Celestis (Gene Roddenberry, Timothy Leary), synthetic diamonds, paint, and coral reefs (Eternal Reefs, about $7,000). Average cremation cost is about $6,000 and an average funeral about $10,000.

segments.title: Ashes statistics and scattering laws
segments.summary: Survey stats show about 40 percent keep ashes at home, 37 percent bury them, water scattering is most popular, and 3 percent go in a columbarium. The National Park Service leaves scattering to each park, the National Forest Service does not regulate, and EPA guidance suggests three miles offshore, though California requires five feet.

segments.title: Famous scatterings and cremation by country
segments.summary: Steve Goodman's ashes were tossed over Wrigley Field by a friend. Graham Parsons' body was stolen and partly burned in Joshua Tree National Park. Cremation rates by country are compared, with Ghana near 3 percent, Hong Kong and Japan high, and the US about 30 percent. Pet cremation is mentioned as a growing, lightly regulated industry.

segments.title: Listener mail
segments.summary: Listener Mark writes about hearing the show in a sauna episode while eating a breakfast sandwich, and Katie from Kent, Washington reports that her betta fish Chucker's Jr. died after jumping out of its bowl.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts ask listeners to send cremation stories to the show email and close the episode.
